title: Space Weather Nowcast
summary_easy: A live browser page that reads nine NOAA space weather feeds, follows the solar wind from a spacecraft 1.58 million km toward the Sun to Earth, and shows how hard it pushes on Earth's magnetic shield, the storm level, and the aurora chance over Syracuse. It was built as the live input side for Tanay's Kp forecasting model. On the measured run the wind was at 360 km/s and would reach Earth 73.5 minutes after it was measured.
summary_deep: sun/app.js polls nine services.swpc.noaa.gov endpoints at 1 to 30 minute cadences into one state object, and sun/helio.js does the logic with no DOM. Plasma and magnetic field are filtered to NOAA's active spacecraft, parsed as UTC, floored to the minute and outer joined, with gaps and source changes reported. Each sample is propagated ballistically with x_GSE from the nearest hourly ephemeris of its own spacecraft over |Vx|. The newest matched sample drives proton dynamic pressure, the Shue et al. (1998) magnetopause standoff against geosynchronous orbit, and the Newell et al. (2007) coupling function. Kp is mapped to the G scale with a rounding rule fitted to NOAA's own forecast labels, provisional 1 minute Kp revisions are counted, OVATION is read at the nearest cell, and the night side comes from an Almanac subsolar point. A two clock freshness model reports each feed's sample age against its own threshold.

sheet.easy:
## What it is
- A live page that follows the solar wind from a spacecraft near the L1 point (about 1.5 million km toward the Sun) to Earth, in the browser, from nine public NOAA feeds.
- It shows the wind's push on Earth's magnetic shield, the storm level (Kp and G scale), solar flares, and the aurora chance over Syracuse.
- Built as the live input side for Tanay's Kp forecasting model, which trained on a clean archive (OMNI2).

## The nine feeds
| Feed | Polled |
| --- | --- |
| Solar wind plasma, magnetic field | every minute |
| Spacecraft positions (ephemeris) | every 30 minutes |
| Kp 1 minute estimate | every minute |
| Kp 3 hour, NOAA scales | every 10 minutes |
| Kp 3 day forecast | every 30 minutes |
| GOES X-ray flux | every minute |
| OVATION aurora | every 5 minutes |

## What it computes
- Travel time to Earth: spacecraft distance divided by the wind's speed toward Earth.
- Pressure of the wind on Earth's field.
- How far out the shield's edge sits (Shue model), against satellites at 6.6 Earth radii.
- How much energy gets in (Newell coupling).
- Freshness of every feed.

## Measured run (Oct 8, 2026, 19:38 UTC)
- Spacecraft SOLAR1 at 1.58 million km; wind 360 km/s, 5.7 protons per cm3.
- Pressure 1.24 nPa, shield edge 10.9 Earth radii, arrival 73.5 minutes after measurement.
- Plasma present in 1,265 of 1,435 minutes. M6.7 flare at 15:48. NOAA forecast peak Kp 5.67 (G2).
- Syracuse aurora chance 0%.

## Lessons
- The spec was wrong about the G scale: NOAA labels Kp 4.67 as G1 because it rounds first.
- NOAA rewrites recent 1 minute Kp values; the page keeps the latest and counts rewrites.
- Hidden tabs got no data until viewed; the first poll now always runs.

## Limits
- Arrival time is approximate by several minutes. Shue is a simple fit. NOAA's forecasts are not scored. Aurora ignores clouds and city light. One quiet day logged.
sheet.deep:
## Architecture
- `sun/helio.js`: pure functions, no DOM, no network. `sun/app.js`: nine polls (30 s timeout, shared backoff) into one state object; handlers only mutate state; one paint job derives everything.
- Base `services.swpc.noaa.gov/`: `json/rtsw/rtsw_wind_1m.json` (1 min), `json/rtsw/rtsw_mag_1m.json` (1 min), `json/rtsw/rtsw_ephemerides_1h.json` (30 min), `json/planetary_k_index_1m.json` (1 min), `products/noaa-planetary-k-index.json` (10 min), `products/noaa-planetary-k-index-forecast.json` (30 min), `products/noaa-scales.json` (10 min), `json/goes/primary/xrays-6-hour.json` (1 min), `json/ovation_aurora_latest.json` (5 min).
- Freshness (sample age, fresh / late): 1 min products 10 / 30 min; ephemeris 4 / 12 h; final Kp 4 / 7 h after window end; OVATION 20 / 60 min after observation time; forecast 3 / 12 h after Last-Modified; scales 3 / 12 h.

## Join
- Only `active === true` rows; `parseUTC` appends Z to zoneless tags; floor to the minute; duplicates keep a valid row; outer join on the minute; per stream count, expected, missing, gaps over 5 min, longest gap, source changes; `matched` needs v, n, Bz, By.

## Propagation
$$\Delta t = \frac{x_{GSE}}{|V_x|}, \qquad t_{arr} = t_{sample} + \Delta t$$
- $x_{GSE}$ from the nearest hourly ephemeris row of the plasma's own spacecraft (binary search); bulk speed if $V_x$ is missing. `arrivingNow` = nearest arrival within 5 min. `streamProgress` = $(t_{now} - t) |V_x| / x_{GSE}$ over the last 2 h.

## Physics
$$P_d\,[\text{nPa}] = 1.6726\times10^{-6}\, n\,[\text{cm}^{-3}]\, v^2\,[\text{km/s}]^2$$
$$r_0 = \left(10.22 + 1.29\tanh\big(0.184(B_z + 8.14)\big)\right) P_d^{-1/6.6}\ [R_E], \quad \alpha = (0.58 - 0.007B_z)(1 + 0.024\ln P_d)$$
$$r(\theta) = r_0\left(\frac{2}{1+\cos\theta}\right)^{\alpha}$$
$$\frac{d\Phi}{dt} = v^{4/3} B_T^{2/3} \sin^{8/3}(\theta_c/2), \quad B_T = \sqrt{B_y^2 + B_z^2}, \quad \theta_c = \operatorname{atan2}(B_y, B_z)$$
- Pressure balance (Chapman and Ferraro) predicts $r_0 \propto P_d^{-1/6}$; Shue fitted 6.6. Geosynchronous orbit 6.6 $R_E$.
- Newell 30 min trailing mean needs 15 samples (two pointer O(n) rolling mean).

## Kp and G
- Kp: 3 hour planetary index, 0 to 9 in thirds; observed, estimated, predicted labels; 1 min estimate is provisional and rewritten (latest wins, revisions counted).
- `kpToG`: strict ($k \ge 5$ is G1) vs noaa ($\mathrm{round}(k + 10^{-9})$ then threshold). Fixture from NOAA's forecast file: 4.67 G1, 5 G1, 5.33 G1, 5.67 G2, 4 and 4.33 none. The test also asserts 8.67 maps to G5 under rounding, which NOAA's scale table (G4 includes 9-) contradicts.
- Visibility by NOAA scale: G2 about 55, G3 about 50, G4 about 45, G5 about 40 degrees geomagnetic latitude.
- Syracuse 43.04 N, 76.13 W geographic; dipole estimate about 52 degrees geomagnetic (pole 80.65 N, 72.68 W, IGRF 2020): $\sin\lambda_m = \sin\lambda\sin\lambda_p + \cos\lambda\cos\lambda_p\cos(\phi - \phi_p)$. Not computed in code.

## Sun and aurora
- Subsolar point (Astronomical Almanac): $L = 280.460 + 0.9856474n$, $g = 357.528 + 0.9856003n$, $\lambda = L + 1.915\sin g + 0.020\sin 2g$, $\varepsilon = 23.439 - 4\times10^{-7}n$; $\delta = \arcsin(\sin\varepsilon\sin\lambda)$; EoT $= L - \alpha_{RA}$; lon $= -15(UT - 12) - $ EoT. Night = more than 90 degrees from it.
- Sun distance $R = 1.00014 - 0.01671\cos g - 0.00014\cos 2g$ AU.
- OVATION: Float32Array 360 x 181, index (lat + 90) x 360 + lon, nearest cell, 10% boundary walking north.
- Flare class: decade letter A to X from 1e-8; multiplier truncated to one decimal; X continues past 10.

| 22 tests (20 physics, 2 util) | README |

## Test strategy
- Closed forms: Pd(5, 400) = 1.338; Shue r0(2, 0) about 10.25 and curve identities; Newell due south and due north; delay 3,750 s.
- NOAA's own labels for the G rule; flare class edges and truncation.
- Astronomy: equinox and solstices of 2026, EoT extremes (+16.4, -14.2 min), sidereal cross check within 0.05 degree, perihelion and aphelion distance.
- Data handling: join with gaps and a source change, derive and arrivingNow, OVATION lookups, Kp windows and chart rows, rolling mean, freshness.

## Limitations
- Ballistic timing (several minutes); Shue symmetric, no dipole tilt; proton only pressure; no forecast archive, no skill score; OVATION nearest cell, no clouds or light; G rounding unverified above 5.67; no persistence; one quiet day logged; the Kp model's top predictors (ap, AE) are absent from these feeds.

narration.script: My Kp forecasting project trained an LSTM on OMNI2, a clean hourly archive that is already shifted to Earth. I wanted to build the input side it would need in production, where the data comes from several spacecraft, at different cadences, with gaps and revisions. The page polls nine NOAA endpoints: solar wind plasma and magnetic field every minute, spacecraft positions hourly, three Kp products, the storm scales, GOES X-ray flux and the OVATION aurora grid. Plasma and field are separate files that list every spacecraft, so I keep only the rows NOAA flags active, floor the time tags to the minute and outer join them. For each minute, I take that spacecraft's sunward distance from the nearest hourly ephemeris and divide by the measured velocity toward Earth. On October 8 that was 1.58 million km at about 358 km/s, so 73.5 minutes. From the newest sample I compute dynamic pressure, 1.24 nanopascals, the Shue magnetopause standoff, 10.9 Earth radii, and the Newell coupling function. Two things surprised me. My spec said Kp 4.67 is below storm level, but NOAA's own forecast file labels it G1, because NOAA rounds first. I followed the file and tested both rules. And NOAA rewrites recent minutes of the 1 minute Kp, so the page keeps the latest value and counts rewrites. Limits: the propagation is ballistic, Shue ignores dipole tilt, and I can't score NOAA's forecasts because the feeds keep no archive. Next, I would store every forecast issue and score it against persistence.

narration.prompt: Give me the full technical story.
narration.script: The starting point was a gap between my Kp model and reality. It trained on OMNI2, which is hourly, cleaned, merged across missions and already propagated to Earth. Live data has none of that done, so I built the layer that does it, in the browser, from nine NOAA endpoints. Solar wind comes from the real time solar wind service as two one minute files, plasma and magnetic field, and each lists every spacecraft NOAA tracks. Exactly one is flagged active at a time. I filter to active rows, parse the zoneless time tags as UTC, because JavaScript would otherwise read them as local time, and floor them to the minute since some sources stamp seconds. Then an outer join on the minute. Plasma drops out much more than the field: on the run, plasma covered 1,265 of 1,435 minutes and field 1,427 of 1,437. An inner join would throw away field data, and an as of join would quietly mix stale density into fresh pressure, so derived quantities use only fully matched minutes. The join reports gaps over five minutes, the longest gap and any change of active spacecraft. Propagation is ballistic. Each sample gets the nearest hourly ephemeris row for its own spacecraft, found by binary search, and the delay is x_GSE over the absolute GSE x velocity. On the run that was 1,581,830 km over 358.6 km/s, 73.5 minutes. I say clearly that this is first order: tilted fronts and a spacecraft well off the Sun Earth line move arrival by several minutes, and the bow shock is met earlier than Earth's centre. From the newest matched sample I compute dynamic pressure, m_p n v squared, which is 1.6726e-6 times n times v squared in the usual units, 1.24 nanopascals. Shue's 1998 model gives the standoff: 10.22 plus 1.29 tanh of 0.184 times Bz plus 8.14, times pressure to the minus 1 over 6.6, which came out at 10.93 Earth radii, drawn against geosynchronous orbit at 6.6. The Newell coupling function, v to the four thirds times the transverse field to the two thirds times sine of half the clock angle to the eight thirds, came out at 4,214. Its 30 minute trailing mean needs 15 samples, so a gap shows as a gap. For Kp, NOAA publishes a one minute estimate, three hour values and a three day forecast with labels. My spec mapped 4.67 to below G1, but the forecast file labels 4.67 G1 and 5.67 G2, because NOAA rounds first. I captured those label pairs as a test fixture. Looking at it again, the test also asserts 8.67 maps to G5, and NOAA's scale table puts 9 minus in G4, so that extrapolation is wrong and I would replace both rules with a lookup. NOAA also rewrites recent one minute values; I keep the latest and count rewrites. The aurora card reads OVATION's one degree grid at the nearest cell and walks north to the first 10% cell, and the night side comes from a subsolar point computed with the Astronomical Almanac formulas, tested at the 2026 equinox and solstices and against a sidereal time cross check. Every feed has a freshness threshold judged on the newest sample inside the file. There are 22 tests, all against closed forms or NOAA's own labels. Limits: ballistic timing, a symmetric magnetopause, no forecast scoring, one quiet day logged, and the Kp model's strongest predictors, ap and the auroral electrojet indices, are not in these feeds at all.

narration.prompt: Explain it to someone without a technical background.
narration.script: The Sun constantly blows a wind of charged particles toward Earth. A spacecraft parked about a million and a half kilometres away, toward the Sun, measures that wind roughly an hour before it hits us. My page reads those measurements live from the US government's space weather centre, works out when each one will reach Earth, and how hard it will push on Earth's magnetic shield. It also shows whether a magnetic storm is expected and the chance of seeing the northern lights over Syracuse. On the day I measured, the wind would arrive about 73 minutes after it was measured, and the chance of aurora over Syracuse was zero. The page also says how fresh each piece of data is, so nobody mistakes old data for live data.

narration.prompt: How do you know the propagation delay is right?
narration.script: I know the arithmetic is right: the test checks 1.5 million km at 400 km/s gives exactly 3,750 seconds, and the run's 73.5 minutes is 1,581,830 km over 358.6 km/s. Whether the wind really arrived then is a different question, and the page does not verify it. Ballistic timing ignores tilted fronts and the spacecraft's offset from the Sun Earth line, so errors of several minutes are normal, and the bow shock responds before Earth's centre. To validate it I would compare predicted arrivals of sharp pressure jumps with sudden commencements on ground magnetometers.

narration.prompt: Why use the GSE x velocity rather than the bulk speed?
narration.script: The delay is about distance along the Sun Earth line, so the relevant speed is the component along that line. The bulk speed includes small sideways components, so it is slightly larger: on the run 360.5 against 358.6 km/s. Dividing by the bulk speed would shorten the delay by about 0.4 minutes here. The code uses Vx when it is present and falls back to bulk speed when it is missing, and the test checks both branches. The difference is small compared with the front tilt error, but it is the correct component.

narration.prompt: What happens when the active spacecraft switches?
narration.script: The join records the source of every minute, reports any change in the active source per stream, and flags a minute whose plasma and field came from different spacecraft. The delay always uses the ephemeris of the plasma's own spacecraft, so a switch from one halo orbit to another changes the distance correctly. The test builds a stream that switches from SOLAR1 to ACE and checks the change is reported. What the page does not do is cross calibrate the two instruments, so a step in density at a switch would pass straight into pressure. On the logged run there were no switches.

narration.prompt: Could you see aurora from Syracuse that night?
narration.script: Almost certainly not, and the page said so. OVATION gave Syracuse 0%, and the nearest 10% cell on its longitude was at 64 degrees north. NOAA's forecast peaked at Kp 5.67, G2, for 06:00 UTC, which is 2 am in Syracuse. Syracuse sits at roughly 52 degrees geomagnetic latitude by a dipole estimate, and NOAA's scale puts G2 visibility around 55 degrees, so at best a faint glow low on the northern horizon. The code works in geographic coordinates and doesn't compute geomagnetic latitude, which is an easy addition.

narration.script: That is true. I fitted the rounding rule to labels from NOAA's forecast file, which only covered 3.67 to 5.67, and then asserted it maps 8.67 to G5. cards.q: Why build this, and how does it connect to the Kp prediction project?
cards.easy: Tanay's Kp forecasting project trained an LSTM on clean hourly history from NASA's OMNI2 archive. A model like that would run in production on live feeds, which come from several spacecraft at different cadences with gaps, revisions and instrument switches. This page builds that live input side.
cards.deep: OMNI2 is a cleaned archive: already shifted from the spacecraft to Earth, merged across missions, with gaps marked. Live RTSW data has none of that done for you: plasma minutes go missing, the active spacecraft label can change mid stream, the ephemeris is hourly and lags the data, and propagation has to be computed before the inputs resemble the training distribution. That gap is training serving skew in its purest form. The page also surfaces a harder problem the method text admits: the Kp model's strongest predictors were ap and the auroral electrojet indices, which are not in these feeds, so a production version needs another source for them or a retrain on solar wind inputs alone.

cards.q: What is the L1 point, and why does a spacecraft there give lead time?
cards.easy: L1 is a balance point about 1.5 million km from Earth toward the Sun, where a spacecraft can stay parked between the two. The solar wind passes it before it reaches Earth, so measurements there arrive roughly 30 to 85 minutes ahead, depending on wind speed.
cards.deep: The first Lagrange point is where the Sun's and Earth's gravity and the centripetal requirement of an orbit with Earth's period balance, about 1% of the way to the Sun. Monitors fly halo or Lissajous orbits around it, so they sit well off the Sun Earth line, and their y and z offsets are in the ephemeris. At 300 to 800 km/s, 1.5 million km takes roughly 30 to 85 minutes. The RTSW files list several spacecraft, which the feed labels ACE, IMAP and SOLAR1, and flag one row per minute as active; the page uses only active rows and shows labels exactly as written. On the run, SOLAR1 was active at x_GSE = 1,581,830 km.

cards.q: How does the page decide whether each feed is current?
cards.easy: Each feed has two clocks. One says whether the last download worked. The other says how old the newest measurement inside the file is, compared with a threshold that fits that product. A feed can download fine and still be stale.
cards.deep: The poll clock lives in the header badges. cards.q: Define solar wind speed, density, the IMF, Bz, Bt and the clock angle. Why does southward Bz matter?
cards.easy: The solar wind is a stream of charged particles from the Sun, typically 300 to 800 km/s with a few protons per cubic centimetre. It carries the Sun's magnetic field (the IMF). Bz is the north south part of that field; when it points south it links up with Earth's field and lets energy in.
cards.deep: Speed is the proton bulk speed (km/s), density the proton number density (cm^-3), temperature the proton temperature. The interplanetary magnetic field is measured in nT; Bx, By, Bz are its components, here in GSM coordinates, Bt is the total field magnitude, and the clock angle theta = atan2(By, Bz) is the field's direction in the y z plane, 0 due north and pi due south. Earth's dayside field points north, so a southward IMF is antiparallel to it at the magnetopause, which favours magnetic reconnection (the Dungey cycle): flux is opened on the dayside, carried over the poles and reconnected in the tail, driving storms and substorms. Northward IMF closes that door. On the run the joined sample had Bz = -1.7 nT and By = 4.01 nT, a mostly dawn dusk field tipped slightly south, and the page colours each minute's dot by Bz.

cards.q: What are GSE and GSM coordinates, and which one does each quantity use?
cards.easy: Both put Earth at the origin with x pointing at the Sun. GSE fixes z to the ecliptic pole. GSM tilts z so that Earth's magnetic dipole lies in the x z plane. Positions and the delay use GSE; the field components that drive Earth's response use GSM.
cards.deep: Geocentric Solar Ecliptic: x toward the Sun, z perpendicular to the ecliptic, y completing the right handed set (toward dusk). Geocentric Solar Magnetospheric: same x, but the x z plane contains the dipole axis, so the frame rocks daily and seasonally relative to GSE. Coupling to the magnetosphere depends on the field relative to the dipole, so Bz and By are read as bz_gsm and by_gsm. Propagation along the Sun Earth line uses the spacecraft's x_gse and the plasma's proton_vx_gse; the two frames share x, so the delay would be the same in either. Mixing frames is a classic bug: Bz in GSE can differ from Bz in GSM by several nT when the dipole tilt is large.

cards.q: How are the plasma and magnetic field files joined?
cards.easy: Both files list every spacecraft. Keep only rows flagged active, round each time stamp down to its minute, and match plasma and field by minute. A minute with only one of the two is kept, with the other half empty, so each chart can use every sample it has.
cards.deep: joinSolarWind(windRows, magRows): rows with active !== true are skipped; time tags are parsed as UTC and floored to the minute, because some sources stamp seconds. Duplicate minutes keep the first row unless it is invalid and a later one is valid (plasma needs proton_speed and proton_density, field needs bz_gsm and by_gsm), and duplicates are counted. Keys from both maps are unioned and sorted: an outer join. Each row records windSource, magSource and a mixed flag when they differ. Per stream it reports count, expected minutes, missing, gaps longer than 5 minutes, the longest gap, and source changes; matched counts minutes with all four of v, n, Bz, By. latestJoined walks back to the newest fully matched minute, and every derived KPI uses it. Tests check active filtering, flooring, sorting, a missing plasma minute kept with NaN, a gap of 8 minutes, and a SOLAR1 to ACE change.

cards.q: Why an outer join on the minute instead of an inner join, or an as of join?
cards.easy: An inner join would throw away good field data whenever plasma is missing, and plasma drops out far more often. Keeping both halves lets the field chart stay complete while anything that needs both (pressure, coupling, standoff) uses only fully matched minutes.
cards.deep: On the run, plasma covered 1,265 of 1,435 minutes while the field covered 1,427 of 1,437, and only the 1,265 matched minutes can feed derived quantities. An inner join would have hidden about 160 field minutes. An as of join (latest plasma at or before each field minute) would fill gaps by carrying old plasma forward and silently mix stale density with fresh field into pressure and coupling, which is exactly the kind of quiet error a nowcast must avoid. Flooring to the minute is a safe key because both products are nominally 1 minute cadences; the cost is that two samples inside one minute collapse to one, which the duplicate counter makes visible. The per row mixed flag catches a minute whose plasma and field came from different spacecraft during a switch.

cards.q: NOAA time tags carry no time zone. What goes wrong, and how does parseUTC fix it?
cards.easy: In JavaScript a date and time string without a zone is read as local time, so a page opened in New York would shift every sample by four or five hours. parseUTC appends a Z, meaning UTC, to any tag that lacks a zone, and turns a space separator into a T.

cards.q: Where does ballistic propagation go wrong?
cards.easy: It assumes the wind travels straight down the Sun Earth line as flat sheets facing Earth. Real fronts are tilted and the spacecraft sits well off that line, so actual arrival can be several minutes earlier or later. It also gives the time to Earth's centre, not to the bow shock.
cards.deep: Errors come from: (1) phase front tilt, where a structure inclined to the Sun Earth line reaches Earth earlier or later depending on the spacecraft's y and z offset; (2) the offset itself, often over 100,000 km for a halo orbit, so the spacecraft may sample a different parcel; (3) distance to the bow shock nose (about 13 to 15 Earth radii upstream), so the magnetosphere responds a few minutes before the computed arrival; (4) evolution of the wind in transit; (5) fast wind overtaking slow wind, where the time mapping stops being one to one and two samples can map to the same arrival, so arrivingNow picks the sample whose arrival is nearest to now within 5 minutes. Better methods estimate the front normal (minimum variance analysis or cross product of fields) and propagate along it, which is what archives like OMNI do.

cards.q: How does the page find the sample reaching Earth now, and how does it draw the stream?
cards.easy: Every minute's measurement gets an arrival time. The one whose arrival is closest to the present, within 5 minutes, is the wind reaching Earth now. In the drawing, each of the last two hours of samples is placed by how far its own speed has carried it since it was measured.
cards.deep: arrivingNow(rows, now, tolMs = 5 min) scans for the minimum |arrival - now| and returns null if the best is more than 5 minutes off, which happens during a plasma gap or when the feed is stale. On the run, the sample measured at 18:24 UTC was arriving at 19:38. streamProgress(rows, now) keeps samples from the last 2 hours and computes km = (now - t) x |Vx| and progress = km / x_GSE; progress 1 is arrival. In the picture the Sun to L1 leg (Almanac Sun distance minus x_GSE) is shortened and the L1 to Earth leg stretched, dots are coloured by Bz on a diverging scale, sized by the square root of density, and spread vertically by a golden ratio sequence of their minute so the height carries no data. A dot meets the Shue magnetopause at its height (shueAtRho, 50 bisection steps) and slides along it.

cards.q: What is dynamic pressure, and where does the constant 1.6726e-6 come from?
cards.easy: Dynamic pressure is how hard the moving wind pushes, like wind on a sail: mass density times speed squared. With density in protons per cubic centimetre and speed in km/s, multiplying by 1.6726e-6 gives nanopascals. On October 8 it was 1.24 nPa.
cards.deep: Pd = m_p n v^2. With m_p = 1.6726e-27 kg, n in cm^-3 (times 1e6 to get m^-3), v in km/s (times 1e3, squared gives 1e6), and Pa to nPa (times 1e9): 1.6726e-27 x 1e6 x 1e6 x 1e9 = 1.6726e-6. So Pd [nPa] = 1.6726e-6 x n x v^2. Check: n = 5, v = 400 gives 1.338 nPa, which the test asserts. Run: 1.6726e-6 x 5.71 x 360.5^2 = 1.241 nPa. Alpha particles (helium nuclei) add a few percent of the mass flux and are often included with a factor near 1.16 to 1.2 in other work, but their columns are empty in these files, so this is proton only pressure and slightly low. Typical quiet values are 1 to 3 nPa; storm compressions reach tens of nPa.

cards.q: State the Shue et al. (1998) magnetopause model and explain each term.
cards.easy: The magnetopause is the boundary where Earth's magnetic field holds off the solar wind. Shue's model gives its distance toward the Sun, r0, from the wind's pressure and Bz: more pressure pushes it in, southward Bz erodes it. A second number, alpha, says how much the flanks flare out.
cards.deep: r0 = (10.22 + 1.29 tanh(0.184 (Bz + 8.14))) Pd^(-1/6.6) Earth radii; alpha = (0.58 - 0.007 Bz)(1 + 0.024 ln Pd); r(theta) = r0 (2 / (1 + cos theta))^alpha, theta measured from the Sun Earth line. The Pd^(-1/6.6) term is close to pressure balance theory: a dipole's magnetic pressure falls as r^-6, so balancing it against ram pressure gives r0 proportional to Pd^(-1/6) (Chapman and Ferraro); the fit found 6.6. The tanh term lowers r0 smoothly as Bz turns south (reconnection removes dayside flux) and saturates for strong Bz either way. alpha grows for southward Bz, so the tail flares more. Run: Pd 1.241, Bz -1.7 gives r0 = 10.93 Re and alpha = 0.595; the test checks Pd 2, Bz 0 gives about 10.25 Re, that r(0) = r0 and r(pi/2) = r0 2^alpha, and that Pd 20 with Bz -10 pushes r0 inside 6.6 Re.

cards.q: What does the Shue model ignore, and why is 6.6 Earth radii drawn beside it?
cards.easy: It is a curve fitted to past spacecraft crossings, symmetric around the Sun Earth line, and it ignores the tilt of Earth's magnetic axis. 6.6 Earth radii is where geostationary satellites orbit; if the standoff drops inside it, satellites near local noon are outside the shield, in the solar wind.
cards.deep: Limits: empirical (no physics simulation), axisymmetric, no dipole tilt or dawn dusk asymmetry, no cusp indentations, and fitted mostly to moderate conditions, though the 1998 version added extreme events. It also uses the latest L1 sample, which reaches Earth one delay later, so the drawn magnetopause is about an hour early unless read with that in mind. Geosynchronous orbit at 6.6 Re is the operational threshold: magnetopause crossings expose satellites to unshielded plasma and can disturb charging and attitude systems. On the run r0 was 10.9 Re and the 24 hour minimum was 10.66 Re at 19:19 UTC (Pd 1.21, Bz -4.5), comfortable margins for a quiet day.

cards.q: What is the Newell coupling function, and why does it use sin to the 8/3 of half the clock angle?
cards.easy: It is a single number for how much energy the solar wind is pushing into Earth's magnetic field right now. It grows with speed and field strength and is zero when the field points due north, largest when it points due south.
cards.deep: dPhi/dt = v^(4/3) Bt^(2/3) sin^(8/3)(theta/2), with Bt = sqrt(By^2 + Bz^2) (transverse field in GSM) and theta = atan2(By, Bz). Newell et al. (2007) fitted this form against ten measures of magnetospheric activity; it is proportional to the rate magnetic flux is opened at the dayside magnetopause. sin(theta/2) is 0 at theta = 0 (north) and 1 at pi (south), and the high 8/3 power makes the function sharply selective for southward fields while still giving By dominated fields some coupling. Units are (km/s)^(4/3) nT^(2/3). Note Bt here excludes Bx, so it differs from the logged total field 4.47 nT. Run: v 360.5, By 4.01, Bz -1.7 gives 4,214. Tests: due south equals v^(4/3) Bt^(2/3), due north is 0, and flipping the sign of By changes nothing.

cards.q: How is the 30 minute Newell mean computed, and why require 15 samples?
cards.easy: It is a trailing average over the previous 30 minutes. If fewer than 15 good samples fall in the window, the point is left blank so a data gap shows as a gap instead of a misleading average of a few minutes.
cards.deep: rollingMean(rows, key, windowMs, minN) keeps a running sum and count with two pointers: add row i if valid, then advance lo while rows[lo].t <= rows[i].t - windowMs, subtracting valid values. Each row is visited at most twice, so it is O(n) instead of O(n w). A point gets sum/n only when n >= minN; the Newell chart uses a 30 minute window with minN = 15, half the expected minutes. Trailing (not centred) means no future data leaks into the value, which matters because the page labels it a predictor that acts on Earth one travel time later. The test checks a point with too few samples is NaN and the later means are exact.

cards.q: What is Kp, and what are the observed, estimated and predicted labels?
cards.easy: Kp is a planet wide score of how disturbed Earth's magnetic field is over a 3 hour block, from 0 (quiet) to 9 (extreme), in thirds. 5 and above is a geomagnetic storm. NOAA labels each block observed, estimated or predicted, and also publishes a provisional estimate every minute.
cards.deep: Each observatory's K index is an integer 0 to 9 from the largest horizontal field fluctuation in a 3 hour UT window, on a quasi logarithmic scale normalised to its latitude. The official planetary Kp is the mean standardised K from 13 observatories between about 44 and 60 degrees geomagnetic latitude; SWPC's real time estimate uses a smaller set of ground magnetometers. Values come in thirds: 4.67 is written 5-, 5.33 is 5+. The forecast product labels windows observed (definitive), estimated (real time), predicted (forecast). The 1 minute estimated Kp is a nowcast and NOAA rewrites its newest minutes. On the run, the 1 minute estimate was 2, and the last 3 hour window was Kp 1.33 from 7 stations.

cards.q: Why does the page not report a skill score for NOAA's Kp forecast?
cards.easy: Scoring a forecast needs the forecasts NOAA made in the past, and these feeds only carry the current one. So the page makes a narrow comparison instead: NOAA's value for the current 3 hour window against the max and mean of the 1 minute estimate so far in that window.
cards.deep: A skill score (for example mean absolute error or a Heidke score against persistence) requires pairs of (forecast issued at time t for window w, observed value for w). products/noaa-planetary-k-index-forecast.json is overwritten on each issue and has no archive of prior issues, so the page cannot build those pairs. Polling it and storing each issue over weeks would allow scoring, but the page keeps no persistent state. kpWindows turns rows into [t0, t0 + 3 h) windows with type and label; windowAt finds the current one; windowStats gives n, max and mean of the 1 minute values inside it; kpChartRows builds step series per type so observed, estimated and predicted steps join without gaps. Claiming skill from one window would be inventing a metric.

cards.q: What is a nowcast versus a forecast, and which parts of this page are which?
cards.easy: A nowcast estimates the current state from the latest measurements; a forecast predicts a future state. The page is mostly a nowcast. The L1 data gives a short look ahead of about an hour, NOAA's OVATION gives aurora roughly 30 to 90 minutes ahead, and the 3 day Kp outlook is NOAA's forecast, shown but not produced by the page.
cards.deep: Nowcasts here: the 1 minute estimated Kp (provisional, from real time magnetometers), the NOAA scales' current levels, current X-ray class, and every quantity computed from the latest L1 sample. The L1 to Earth propagation is a physics based look ahead: it predicts conditions at Earth one travel time later by assuming the measured wind persists unchanged in transit, so pressure, standoff and coupling shown now act on Earth about 73 minutes later. OVATION is a model forecast with lead time set by the L1 travel time; the file states an observation time and a forecast time (19:29 and 20:45 on the run, 76 minutes apart). The Kp forecast is NOAA's 3 day product. Beyond about an hour, prediction needs models of the Sun and heliosphere, not L1 data.

cards.q: How does Kp relate to how far south the aurora reaches?
cards.easy: As Kp rises, the auroral oval expands toward the equator. NOAA's scale page gives rough visibility by storm level: G2 (Kp 6) to about 55 degrees geomagnetic latitude, G3 (Kp 7) about 50, G4 (Kp 8) about 45, G5 (Kp 9) about 40. Aurora low on the northern horizon can be seen from farther south than the oval itself.
cards.deep: The oval sits around 65 to 70 degrees geomagnetic latitude in quiet times. Stronger driving (southward Bz, high speed) loads more open flux into the tail, enlarging the polar cap and pushing the oval's equatorward edge to lower latitudes, and Kp, built from mid latitude magnetometers, tracks that disturbance. The relation is statistical and uses geomagnetic latitude, not geographic. SWPC notes aurora can be seen up to about 1,000 km from the visible oval when it is bright, which is why a place south of the oval can still see a glow low on the horizon. OVATION replaces the Kp rule of thumb with a model driven by L1 solar wind, giving probability on a 1 degree geographic grid; if solar wind input is missing it falls back on Kp.

cards.q: What is Syracuse's geomagnetic latitude, and does the code use it?
cards.easy: The code does not compute it. It stores Syracuse in geographic coordinates (43.04 N, 76.13 W) and reads OVATION's geographic grid. With a dipole approximation and the 2020 geomagnetic pole near 80.65 N, 72.68 W, Syracuse sits at about 52 degrees geomagnetic latitude, between the G2 and G3 visibility lines.
cards.deep: Geomagnetic (dipole) latitude: sin(lat_m) = sin(lat) sin(lat_p) + cos(lat) cos(lat_p) cos(lon - lon_p), where (lat_p, lon_p) is the north geomagnetic pole. With lat 43.04, lon -76.13, pole 80.65 N, 72.68 W: 0.6826 x 0.9867 + 0.7308 x 0.1625 x cos(3.45 deg) is about 0.792, so lat_m is about 52.4 degrees (an estimate computed for this card, not a project result). Because the pole is tilted toward North America, Syracuse is about 9 degrees further 'north' magnetically than geographically. By NOAA's table, aurora overhead would need roughly G3 (Kp 7, about 50 degrees), and G2 (about 55 degrees) gives at best a low horizon glow. cards.q: How is the night side shaded on the aurora map?
cards.easy: The page computes where the Sun is directly overhead (the subsolar point) from low precision formulas in the Astronomical Almanac. Everything more than 90 degrees from that point is night. On the run the Sun was overhead at 6.11 S, 117.77 W.
cards.deep: subsolarPoint(date): days from J2000 n; mean longitude L = 280.460 + 0.9856474 n; mean anomaly g = 357.528 + 0.9856003 n; ecliptic longitude lambda = L + 1.915 sin g + 0.020 sin 2g; obliquity eps = 23.439 - 0.0000004 n; declination = asin(sin eps sin lambda); right ascension = atan2(cos eps sin lambda, cos lambda). Equation of time (EoT) = L - RA in degrees (4 minutes per degree), the gap between clock noon and solar noon. Subsolar longitude = -15 (UT - 12) - EoT. A sidereal time route (RA - GMST) gives the same longitude and is kept as a cross check. The Almanac quotes about 0.01 degree accuracy for 1950 to 2050. The terminator is geometric, with no refraction or twilight, so it is a slightly generous night. Run: subsolar 6.11 S, 117.77 W, EoT +12.56 minutes, which fits early October.

cards.q: How are GOES X-ray flare classes defined, and how does the code compute them?
cards.easy: Flares are graded by peak X-ray brightness in the 0.1 to 0.8 nm band. Each letter is a factor of ten: A, B, C, M, X from 1e-8 to 1e-4 watts per square metre. The number is the multiple of the letter's base, so 3.2e-5 is M3.2.
cards.deep: flareClass(flux): level by decade (A below 1e-7, B below 1e-6, C below 1e-5, M below 1e-4, otherwise X), multiplier = floor(flux / base x 10 + 1e-6) / 10, truncated rather than rounded so 9.99e-6 is C9.9 and never C10.0, and X continues past 10 (1.23e-3 is X12.3). A decade edge belongs to the upper class (1e-6 is C1.0). The handler groups rows by time, keeping the 0.1 to 0.8 nm 'long' channel with its satellite number and the 0.05 to 0.4 nm 'short' channel with NOAA's electron contamination flag (read under the key spelled electron_contaminaton in the file). Flares drive the R (radio blackout) scale, separate from G. Run: C1.1 at 19:35 from GOES-18, and an M6.7 earlier at 15:48 UTC.

cards.q: Your spec was wrong about the G scale. What happened?
cards.easy: The spec said Kp 4.67 counts as below G1, a strict threshold at 5. NOAA's own forecast file labels 4.67 as G1 and 5.67 as G2, because NOAA rounds Kp to the nearest whole number first. The page now follows NOAA, keeps both rules, and tests both.
cards.deep: The discovery came from reading the data rather than the documentation: the forecast file carries a noaa_scale label beside each Kp, and on October 8 the file labelled 5.67 as G2, where the strict rule says G1. The correct response was to treat NOAA's labels as ground truth for what NOAA publishes, capture the (kp, label) pairs as a fixture, and require the implementation to reproduce them, while keeping the strict rule because some users read the scale that way and the method section explains the choice. The same test also asserts 8.67 maps to G5 under rounding, which NOAA's own scale table contradicts (it lists 9- under G4), so the lesson is only half applied: validate against the source's labels everywhere you assert, not just where you captured them.
cards.say: My spec said 4.67 is below G1. NOAA's own forecast file labels 4.67 as G1 and 5.67 as G2, because NOAA rounds first. So I followed the file, kept both rules and tested both. Looking again, my test extends the rounding rule to 8.67 without a label to check it, and NOAA's table disagrees there.

Two things make this bug easy to miss: developers test in a focused tab, and browsers throttle timers in background tabs anyway, so the symptom looks like a slow network. The fix keeps the bandwidth saving for long idle tabs while removing the empty first impression.

Separating ingestion from painting means nine feeds arriving at different times cause one repaint per frame at most, and painting can pause without losing data. The location choice is kept in localStorage inside a try, since storage can be blocked. cards.q: What are the honest limitations?
cards.easy: Ballistic propagation is only approximate. The Shue model is a symmetric empirical fit. NOAA's past forecasts cannot be scored from these feeds. OVATION is read at the nearest one degree cell, and clouds and light pollution are ignored.
cards.deep: (1) Arrival uncertain by several minutes (tilted fronts, off line spacecraft, bow shock upstream, evolution in transit). (2) Shue: no dipole tilt, no asymmetry, uses the L1 sample about an hour before it acts. (3) No forecast archive, so no skill score. (4) OVATION nearest cell; geographic location only, no geomagnetic latitude computed; no cloud, moon or city light. (5) Proton only dynamic pressure (alpha columns empty). (6) The G scale rounding rule is unverified above 5.67 and conflicts with NOAA's table at 9-. (7) No persistence: revision counts and history reset on reload, and the 1 minute Kp map keeps one day. (8) One snapshot run on a quiet day; no storm time behaviour has been logged.
evidence: portfolio: Ballistic propagation is approximate. Solar wind fronts are tilted, so the real arrival can differ by several minutes.

cards.q: What would it take to feed this into the Kp prediction model in production?
cards.easy: Store the live inputs over time, propagate and resample them the way the training archive was built, check they match the training distribution, and find a source for the model's strongest inputs, which these feeds do not carry.
cards.deep: Steps: (1) persist every fetch with its fetch time (append only), keeping revisions, so features can be rebuilt as of any moment and training uses the same as of view; (2) reproduce OMNI style processing: propagate to the bow shock nose, average to hourly, apply the same gap rules, so online features match offline ones; (3) monitor drift between live and archive distributions (speed, density, Bz quantiles); (4) handle spacecraft switches, which shift calibration; (5) solve the missing predictors: the Kp model's strongest inputs were ap and the auroral electrojet indices, which are derived from ground magnetometers and are effectively current state, so either ingest a real time source or retrain on solar wind only, accepting lower skill; (6) define fallbacks when plasma drops out, since the run showed about 12% of minutes missing. Without step 2 the model would see a different input distribution than it was trained on.

cards.q: What breaks at 10x and 100x scale?
cards.easy: One browser tab polling nine files is fine. If thousands of people opened it, NOAA would see thousands of identical requests a minute; at that point the right design is one server that polls once, stores history, and serves everyone.
cards.deep: 10x in data (longer history, more spacecraft, higher cadence): the in memory arrays and O(n) joins still work, but repainting full 24 hour charts every minute gets heavy; incremental appends and downsampling help. 100x in users: every client polling services.swpc.noaa.gov is wasteful and impolite to a public service; a backend should poll once, normalise and version the data, and push updates to clients over server sent events or a CDN cached JSON. 100x in history: a time series store keyed by (feed, minute, fetch time) to keep revisions, plus precomputed rollups. Forecast scoring becomes possible once issues are archived. Alerting (r0 below 6.6 Re, G3 forecast for Syracuse) needs a server anyway, because a closed tab cannot alert.

cards.q: What would you do next?
cards.easy: Archive NOAA's forecasts so they can be scored. Add geomagnetic latitude for locations. Improve propagation for tilted fronts. And log a real storm day.
cards.deep: (1) A small backend that stores every forecast issue and every 1 minute Kp version, then scores the forecast against later estimated and observed Kp with persistence as the baseline. (2) Compute geomagnetic latitude (AACGM or IGRF dipole) for each place and show the NOAA visibility lines against it. (3) Replace the G rules with a thirds notation lookup validated against NOAA's table and more captured labels. (4) Propagation along an estimated front normal, compared with ballistic arrival using ground magnetometer sudden commencements as truth. (5) Include alpha particles when the columns are populated. (6) Run the page through a geomagnetic storm and log how coverage, revisions and freshness behave under stress, since every logged number so far comes from a quiet day.

cards.q: Ballistic propagation is crude. Why not a proper model?
cards.easy: For an hour ahead of a single point at Earth, ballistic timing is the standard first order method and its error, several minutes, is stated on the page. Better methods need front orientation estimates, and a full heliospheric model answers a different question, days ahead from the Sun.
cards.deep: Concede: tilted fronts and spacecraft offsets cause errors of several minutes, and OMNI style processing does better. Defend: the page uses the real ephemeris distance and the measured x velocity per sample, not constants; it marks the sample arriving now with a 5 minute tolerance; and it says plainly that the delay is to Earth's centre and the bow shock is met earlier. A model like WSA-Enlil propagates from the Sun over days and is not the tool for the last 1.5 million km. Next step would be front normal propagation, validated against sudden commencements.
cards.say: It is first order, and the page says arrival can be off by several minutes. It does use the real spacecraft distance and each minute's own velocity, which already beats a constant one hour shift. If I improved it, I'd estimate the front orientation and check arrivals against sudden commencements on ground magnetometers.

cards.q: Shue 1998 is an old empirical fit. Why use it?
cards.easy: It is still the most widely used simple magnetopause model, it takes exactly the two inputs available live (pressure and Bz), and it has a closed form that runs instantly in a browser. Its limits, symmetry and no dipole tilt, are written on the page.
cards.deep: Concede: newer models add dipole tilt, asymmetry and cusp indentations, and an MHD simulation would be more faithful. Defend: the page's job is a live standoff estimate against the 6.6 Re geosynchronous line, where Shue's r0 is a standard reference; the formula is tested against its closed form and its identities; and the Pd^(-1/6.6) scaling agrees with pressure balance theory. A newer model would change r0 by fractions of an Earth radius on a quiet day like the logged one (10.9 Re), which matters less than getting the inputs and timing right.
cards.say: Shue is the standard simple model, and it needs only pressure and Bz, which are exactly what I have live. It's closed form, so it runs in a browser and is easy to test. The page says it ignores dipole tilt. On a quiet day with the edge near 11 Earth radii, the model choice matters less than the inputs and timing.

cards.q: NOAA already publishes all of this. What did you add?
cards.easy: NOAA publishes the raw feeds and its own products; the joining, propagation, derived physics and freshness checks are this page's work. Pressure, the magnetopause standoff, coupling and the per sample arrival time are computed here, and each feed's age is judged against its own threshold.
cards.deep: Concede: Kp, the forecast, OVATION, X-ray flux and the scales are NOAA's numbers, displayed rather than produced. Defend: the integration layer is the point, because it is what a model needs in production: active spacecraft filtering, minute joins with gap and source change reporting, ephemeris based delay per sample, provisional value revision counting, and sample age monitoring. Building it surfaced two real findings: the G scale reading NOAA's labels imply, and NOAA rewriting recent 1 minute Kp values.
cards.say: NOAA gives me the raw feeds and some products. What I built is the integration: picking the active spacecraft, joining plasma and field by minute, propagating each sample with the real spacecraft distance, and checking every feed's freshness. That's the layer a model would need, and building it is how I found NOAA rewriting recent Kp minutes.

cards.q: Rounding Kp to match one file is overfitting to a single snapshot.
cards.easy: Partly fair. The rule was fitted to seven label pairs from one capture, all between 3.67 and 5.67. It explains every label seen, and NOAA's scale table supports it at 5-, but the table contradicts it at 9-, so it is not a validated general rule.
cards.deep: Concede: one capture, a narrow range, and an untested extrapolation that the test then asserts (8.67 as G5). Defend: the choice was evidence based rather than guessed, both readings are implemented and tested, and the method text explains the difference so a reader can see which one is in use. The right fix is a lookup on the thirds notation checked against NOAA's scale table and more captured labels across storm levels.
cards.say: Partly fair. I fitted it to seven label pairs from one capture, and they only go up to 5.67. It explains everything I saw, but NOAA's table puts 9 minus in G4 and my rule says G5. The fix is a lookup on the thirds notation, checked against the table.

cards.q: One run on a quiet day proves nothing about a nowcast.
cards.easy: Agreed that it is one snapshot, and the write up presents it as one. It shows the pipeline producing correct, internally consistent numbers from real feeds; behaviour during a storm, when the page matters most, has not been logged.
cards.deep: Concede: Kp 2, r0 near 11 Re, no source switch, no storm. Defend: every derived value in the log can be recomputed by hand from the logged inputs (1.6726e-6 x 5.71 x 360.5^2 = 1.241 nPa; 1,581,830 / 358.6 s = 73.5 minutes), the formulas are tested against closed forms, and the join and revision logic are tested on synthetic gaps and source changes. The missing evidence is a storm day, with high speed, strongly southward Bz, possible spacecraft switches and rapid Kp revisions, and that is on the next list.
cards.say: Yes, it's one snapshot on a quiet day, and I present it that way. What it shows is the pipeline giving consistent numbers I can recompute by hand from the logged inputs. What it doesn't show is storm behaviour, which is when a nowcast matters, so logging a storm day is next.

cards.q: Why not just hit NOAA every minute from a server instead of from each browser?
cards.easy: For a portfolio dashboard with a handful of viewers, browser polling needs no infrastructure and the feeds are public, cached and small. With real traffic it would be the wrong design, and a single poller with fan out would replace it.
cards.deep: Concede: per client polling multiplies load on a public service and loses history on reload. Defend: cadences are matched to each product's update rate (hourly ephemeris every 30 minutes, forecast every 30, OVATION every 5), polling stops for hidden tabs after the first fetch, failures back off exponentially, and fetches time out at 30 s. The pure helio.js module would move to a server unchanged, which is the payoff of keeping it free of DOM code.
cards.say: For a few viewers it's the simplest thing that works, and the cadences match how often each product changes. With real traffic I'd poll once on a server, store every version, and push to clients. The physics module has no page code, so it would move to the server unchanged.

cards.q: Explain this project to a hiring manager in under a minute.
cards.easy: A live space weather page that integrates nine NOAA feeds into the inputs a forecasting model would need.
cards.deep: Problem (live inputs for a model trained on clean history), what it does, one number, one finding.
cards.say: I had built a Kp forecasting model on clean archive data, and I wanted to see what feeding it live would take. So I built a page that joins nine NOAA feeds, propagates solar wind from a spacecraft 1.58 million km out to Earth, and computes the physics that drives storms. On the measured run the wind would reach Earth in 73.5 minutes. Building it showed me the model's best predictors aren't in the live feeds at all.
evidence: portfolio: found the spacecraft labelled SOLAR1 active at 1.58 million km sunward

cards.q: Explain the data integration to a staff engineer.
cards.easy: Active row filtering, minute flooring, outer join, ephemeris lookup by binary search, latest value wins for revised minutes, and per feed sample age monitoring.
cards.deep: Cover join keys, why outer, propagation per sample, revision handling, and the two clock freshness model.
cards.say: Plasma and field come in separate files that list every spacecraft, so I keep only active rows, floor time tags to the minute and outer join them, which keeps field data when plasma drops out. Each sample gets the nearest hourly ephemeris of its own spacecraft and a delay of x over Vx. Kp minutes that NOAA rewrites are overwritten and counted. Freshness is judged on the newest sample inside each file, not on whether the fetch worked.

cards.q: Explain to a product manager why the page shows data freshness so prominently.
cards.easy: A live dashboard that silently shows old data is worse than one that shows nothing, so each feed's sample age is a first class display.
cards.deep: Frame it as trust: a download can succeed while the data inside is hours old.
cards.say: A feed can download fine and still contain hour old data, and a space weather page that looks live but isn't can mislead someone checking for aurora tonight. So every feed shows two things: did the last fetch work, and how old is the newest measurement inside it. Each has its own threshold, because the ephemeris updates hourly while the wind updates every minute.

cards.q: Explain to a recruiter what this project shows about you.
cards.easy: It shows multi source data integration, physics models implemented and tested from the papers, and honesty about what the data can and cannot claim.
cards.deep: Plain words: joins live data, implements science, checks its work, admits limits.
cards.say: It shows I can take several messy live data sources and turn them into numbers people can trust. I implemented published physics models, tested them against known answers, and found a place where my own spec disagreed with how NOAA labels storms. I also say what the page can't do, like scoring NOAA's forecasts, because the data to do that isn't there.
